paragraphs: After both armies had regrouped, they watched each other across the Fei River for seven more days. Brown ridges of sand appeared in the shallows, while boats could still pass through the deeper channels. By day Qin crossbow carts stood in rows on the dry ground, and Beifu skiffs moved through the branches of the river. At night the watchmen’s clappers answered one another across the water. Sometimes the same waterbird’s cry was taken by the eastern bank for a signal from its own scouts, and by the western bank for the approach of an enemy. Morning came before either side could be certain.

Fu Rong had the shoals measured every day. Age was advancing, and his old wound hurt whenever the cold came, yet he still inspected the wheel tracks where crossbow carts climbed the slopes. Three small flags were ready along the sandbar: a blue border meant form ranks, yellow meant redeploy the camp, red meant halt pursuit. Many recruits had never seen this system of signals. Veterans taught them to distinguish the flags while mocking the young men for being frightened even to look at the Heavenly King’s military code. Fu Rong overheard. He merely had one laughing veteran fetch his own squad flag and recite its signals with his back turned. The man made two mistakes and stopped laughing.

When Fu Jian climbed the command platform, Fu Rong pointed out a stretch of wetland downstream. Cavalry could barely pass through it in a column, with no room to turn. If Liu Yu came that way, Qin horsemen would block one another as soon as they gave chase. Fu Jian asked whether his brother had slept the night before. Fu Rong said only that his leg ached, waking him often enough to study the military map twice.
“You still remember twenty years ago,” Fu Jian said.

Fu Rong looked up into the gray fog over the southern shore. Wang Meng had not long been dead then, and everyone had said that a single edict was all that stood between them and crossing south. He remembered counting a million troops for his imperial brother, and how those numbers, item by item, had become measures of grain and the faces of conscripted laborers. The river remained. The commander across it had changed. Much inside their own army had changed as well.
“I remember,” he replied. “If the lines had broken here that year, I doubt any of us would have found the others.”

Fu Jian did not return to the past. He ordered the rear-camp beacon signals checked again: if a granary caught fire, the forward units were not to spread a report of defeat on their own authority. Fu Rong inspected the flagmen personally, then summoned the reserve commandants of the left and right camps before returning to his tent. He asked each who would take command if the commanding officer fell. Anyone who answered incorrectly was sent back to drill.

On the southern bank, Liu Yu spread a mud map of the battlefield across a mat. His generals reported that the provisions would last ten days with some margin, but medicines were especially scarce. Two boats carrying salt from Jingkou had lain upstream for three nights before being permitted through. Jiankang urged him to pull south and guard the Yangtze. Many Jin ministers, meanwhile, demanded the recovery of the three towns: having restored the Jin dynasty, they said, how could they allow Qin troops to stand on its old soil?
He Wuji set the two sets of urgent court dispatches aside. “If we win today, every one of them will say he proposed it first. If we lose, there’ll be a crowd asking why we were greedy for glory.”

Liu Yu pressed down the letters with his hand. “Don’t argue their case for them yet. Delay any longer and the boatmen will scatter, the crossbows won’t be replenished, and then we won’t be able to hold the line either.”

He made the units report their experienced oarsmen, armored men able to swim, and remaining fire oil, and asked who could read Qin’s flags. An elderly defector said he had served at Luoyang years ago and recognized the old army’s red banners. It emerged that new-camp signals were different: of ten flags he could name only four correctly. Liu Yu reassigned him to identifying the seals on grain boats and had scouts verify the flags instead.

The attack plan was straightforward. They would first send an envoy asking Qin to move its forward camp two li back from the shallows and agree to a pitched battle after noon. Two flotillas would cross, light troops seizing the bank while the elite pushed past the outposts toward Qin’s center. Farther upstream, several boats would hide in the reeds and light smoke fires when the main force crossed. If the fires sowed doubts between Qin’s front and rear, the Beifu Army might seize a brief opening.
An old general was uneasy. “Twenty years ago Xie Xuan asked them to yield the bank too. Fu Jian refused.”
“If he refuses, we’ll choose another crossing,” Liu Yu replied. “If he agrees, that doesn’t mean he’s taken the bait. Whenever a formation moves, some part of men’s confidence loosens with it.”
“Fu Rong commands their center,” He Wuji said.

Liu Yu stopped the tip of his knife above the middle of the mud map. When he had been a commoner in Jingkou, he had heard elders recount how Fu Rong helped the Heavenly King bring the north together. Now, having seen Qin’s formations for himself, he could not deny the foundations laid by years of training. Yet he wished to test them: if that commander fell, could the tens of thousands behind him hold their stations by camp signal alone?

The envoy crossed the next morning. Jin’s letter requested that Qin withdraw its shallow-water forward camp two li before noon and allow the Jin army to cross for battle. Qin’s tent rang with laughter. One man said Liu Yu treated Xie Xuan’s old stratagem like a new secret; another urged that they let the Jin cross and then shoot them. Fu Jian read the letter and ordered the forward camp moved back the requested distance. Baggage trains went first, crossbow carts afterward; at every stage one unit stopped, turned to face south, and only then drew the next unit back. The right wing prepared horsemen on dry ground, forbidden to reinforce without an explicit command from the center.
Fu Rong looked at his brother. “Liu Yu won’t wait until we’re formed before he crosses.”
“I know.”
“He wants to see whether we can retreat in order.”

Fu Jian picked up a camp marker and set it near the high ground. “If we cannot withdraw two li in good order, how will we command an army when the roads between north and south grow longer still? You hold the center. I shall watch the wings from the platform.”

The forward units left the shallows, their wheels grinding slowly through soft ground. Hearing the first war drums from the far bank, several new soldiers could not help turning their heads. Squad leaders pushed them forward with the backs of their shields and ordered them to match the steps of their comrades. One Qin banner came down; another spread on the slope behind it. Watching from his tower ship, Liu Yu saw the Qin army as a series of gates, one closing back to reveal another.

After noon the drums quickened. Jin boats rushed toward the shoals with the wind, bolts passing over their wet felt screens and lodging in the stockades. The water reached their knees. Beifu troops abandoned their skiffs, hoisted shields, and waded up through the mud. Qin’s first line had withdrawn but was shooting down from the rise. Many in the first landing party fell, while those behind pushed the boats forward through the water to shelter their comrades. Liu Yu walked along the gunwale to the bow, blood spattering his face, still urging the oarsmen to bring the second contingent ashore.

Thick smoke suddenly rose behind a tributary. Beifu men had set fire to dried reeds and several worn-out wooden boats. The flames were small, but the wind blew smoke into Qin’s rear camp. Men wearing Qin armor scavenged from earlier battlefields mingled with the wagon crews and shouted that the rear granary had fallen and Jin troops had crossed upstream. An arrow cart broke an axle and overturned at the slope; a frightened horse tore loose and crashed into a line of crossbowmen. A squad of young Qin soldiers, believing their escape route severed, surged toward the camp banner and broke apart a rank that had only just formed.
“The rear has been defeated!” The cry rose and fell in the smoke.

Qin’s blue-bordered flag immediately dipped halfway, then unfurled toward the front. By regulation it ordered a shield formation; men who did not know the signal thought the main flag was falling. Two reserve commandants took orders separately and barred the frightened packhorses from the infantry ranks. While the front still hesitated, the rear planted its shields in the mud and formed a horizontal line by squad. A squad leader found a Jin camp tablet under the clothing of a man screaming that all was lost. He bound the man and handed him to the military magistrate rather than beheading him in anger.

The disorder had only half subsided when the Beifu elite reached them. Liu Yu broke through the front stockade, leapt past the burning fence, and drove straight for the “Yangping” banner in the center of the high ground. He Wuji advanced to his right, taking his marines to block a slope used by Qin’s crossbow carts, forcing several of the machines to turn awkwardly and lose their field of fire.

In their light armor, the Beifu troops moved faster through the narrow space than Qin’s heavy infantry. Blades stabbed through gaps in shields at such close quarters that men saw white froth on their opponents' lips. After shields splintered and spears snapped, some fought with loose iron plates torn from their own armor. Others slipped into the mud and were hauled up by their squadmates, half a leg soaked red.

Fu Rong ordered the two flanking camps to hold their original banners. His guards urged him to remain on the height: signals alone could direct the battle. But he saw new recruits searching the smoke for the center. If their commander stayed hidden now, some would doubt him even with every order intact. He mounted and advanced with a Yangping banner for two hundred paces behind the lines, reconnecting the scattered crossbowmen to the shield infantry.
“Don’t crowd toward the center!” he shouted. “If your own camp breaks, the center will break with it!”

A troop of Di cavalry saw the Jin break in and tried to charge out by a shortcut, only to be stopped by a military magistrate with drawn sword. They cursed him for cowardice. White-faced, he still barred the timber gate, telling them that horses trampling the front line’s shield ranks would be killing their own men for the enemy. The troop leader resented the order but eventually turned back and re-formed his horsemen.

As Fu Rong crossed a drainage ditch, an arrow flew through the turmoil and struck his mount in the chest. The horse reared violently, its forelegs folded, and it pitched sideways into the mud. Fu Rong’s left foot reached the earth, but his right was twisted into the stirrup leather and trapped beneath the horse. His shoulder armor struck so hard that his sight went white. Hot blood spread along his knee guard, and for a moment the weight on his chest stopped his breath. Jin soldiers saw the fallen horse and immediately cried that Fu Rong was dead.

The drums drew closer through the mud. Suddenly he recognized the horn of his own central army. Twenty years earlier on this riverbank he had dreamed of being trampled by soldiers in flight; he had woken in Chang’an with the palace candles still burning. Now he lay in the mud in truth, without time to tell dream from death. A man thrust a shield over him to fend off a descending spear. The shield took a sword blow and nearly split in two.
“Lord of Yangping! Can you still speak?” the man roared.

Through mud-streaked brows Fu Rong recognized Liang Hu. When the First Battalion was newly formed, Liang Hu had been a young cavalryman forever cursing at the camp gate, the wolf’s fang at his waist polished bright. Now gray flecked his temples. His horsemanship and archery remained steady, though the arm holding the shield trembled with strain. Seeing Fu Rong open his eyes, he shouted behind him, “Manu! Cut the stirrup! Don’t pull his leg!”

Manu was an old Qiang soldier whose archery had weakened; he now kept the camp’s flag tallies. At the shout he threw himself forward and severed the stirrup leather with his blade. Zhai Hei knelt in the mud on the other side, thrusting his shoulder under the dead horse’s belly; two new Dingling recruits lifted as he gestured. Zhao An came up with Han crossbowmen and, without stopping to ask whether the commander lived, ordered them to press the Jin back. Each man called out his name as the weapons were reloaded; their clear voices carried over the clash of blades.
“Heave!” Liang Hu knelt on one knee with the shield raised, blood running from the seams of his left arm guard. “We’ve all lifted wagons together. Can’t we lift one dead horse today?”

They clenched their teeth and raised the horse a fraction. Manu dragged Fu Rong outward. Pain left the commander barely able to breathe; gripping Manu’s shoulder armor, he heard an old Qiang curse and found it strangely dear. Zhai Hei strained once more beneath the carcass, and at last they drew Fu Rong free. Liang Hu turned toward the standard-bearer. Arrows had pierced the Yangping banner in several places and its pole was beginning to tilt. He ordered a squad to take hold. The flagman had an arrow through his left arm but had not released the pole. A young Xianbei beside him caught the banner’s trailing edge and braced the shaft with his body to keep it from falling into the mud.

“Lord Yangping lives!” Liang Hu cried until his voice grew hoarse. Zhao An ordered the news passed by camp signals and forbade men to run about shouting. The banner remained standing, the wounded commander was dragged behind the line, and neither flank changed its orders. Rumors gradually stopped reaching the front, even as the Beifu battle cries drew nearer.

Liu Yu attacked three times in succession. By the third charge some of the soldiers beside him had nicked their blades beyond use, and their shield arms shook. Qin crossbow carts kept the Jin boats near shore under fire, delaying reinforcements. Though the Beifu elite drove Qin’s line back more than ten paces, the central banner never withdrew. Through the crowd Liu Yu saw men dragging the dead horse away behind the formation and others planting the Yangping standard firmly once more. He knew the moment that mattered most had passed.

From the Qin command platform, Fu Jian had also seen his brother fall. A mounted messenger stumbled onto the steps twice, first reporting the general’s fate unknown, then saying he had been rescued and carried behind the lines. Fu Jian asked whether the center had lowered its flags or either wing moved without orders. Neither had. Princes at his side urged him to send cavalry and drive the Beifu troops into the river. He gripped the railing until his knuckles turned blue. Twenty years younger, he knew, he might have drawn his sword and rushed down the slope the instant his brother fell. But the narrow waterways still lay where the map showed them, as did the approaches Murong Chui had circled while ill.
“Hold according to the flags,” he said. “The upstream force must stay on the dry road. Don’t lead it into the paddies merely to rescue the center.”

An attendant asked whether the emperor would not ride forward himself if Fu Rong truly had been killed. Fu Jian glanced at the officer kneeling for orders before the platform. “If he is dead, there is all the less reason to let ten more battalions die with him.”

At last smoke signals came from upstream. Qin infantry and cavalry dispatched beforehand along the dry road had taken the high ground by Shiliang Ferry, cutting a reserve Beifu supply route and threatening the landing places behind the Jin attack. They did not pursue across the river into the Jin main camp. Instead they fenced off shore where Jin boats might have docked and burned the military mooring ropes prepared there. Two Jin scouts rode back on horses almost too exhausted to move and brought the news to Liu Yu’s front.

He Wuji came to request a withdrawal, saying the boats still at the bank could not withstand another assault. Liu Yu gazed at the Qin platform. Fu Jian, he understood, was waiting for him to spend all his strength; the Qin emperor would no longer be lured down onto wet ground chosen by the Jin. The Beifu Army could still fight, but it could not risk the entire force in one breach.
“The vanguard becomes the rearguard,” he ordered. “The gravely wounded go first. Boats receive men by their numbers. No crowding. Bind anyone who tries to seize a boat out of turn.”

The Jin sounded the gong to retreat. Several young Qin generals urged an advance to exploit their success. Fu Jian ordered the red flags raised first. Horsemen were to stop north of the shoals, and crossbowmen could fire only to suppress armed resistance, not loose volleys into the beaten soldiers crowded aboard the boats. A man who had lost his brother wept that they were allowing his killer to escape. His squadmates held him back. His officer, himself wounded, used the flat of his sword to knock back those crossing the line.

Liu Yu remained aboard the last skiff. Qin soldiers did not swarm into the river in pursuit. Instead they lifted their own wounded and also several Jin men left on the shoals. He saw the Yangping banner, shot through so badly the light passed through it, still held upright in the wind. The oarsman beside him suddenly asked, “General, will they come tonight?”
“They’ll come along the roads,” Liu Yu replied. “But they won’t slaughter us in the river tonight.”

The sun sank behind the western bank. Broken spears and fragments of boats drifted downstream. Qin soldiers separated captured wounded men by camp and physicians treated them according to the gravity of their injuries. One Qin man protested that his own squadmate was still waiting for his bleeding to be stopped. The physician sharply ordered him to carry in the two most seriously wounded men first and stop arguing at the gate over which state’s armor they wore.

Fu Jian went in person to the wounded men’s camp. He saw Liang Hu’s split shield, the sleeve of Manu’s tunic darkened with blood, bruises across Zhai Hei’s shoulder; Zhao An was still registering the names of those unaccounted for, one by one. Fu Jian ordered only that those involved in the rescue have their actions recorded in their own units' merit registers. Rewards and penalties would be checked by army command; no one was to be promoted over ranks on the spot.

Fu Rong woke once. His first words asked about the banner. Fu Jian told him it still stood. Fu Rong asked whether the Jin had withdrawn; hearing they had evacuated by boat number, he finally relaxed his frown. His wounds hurt too much for laughter, but he insisted on knowing who had saved him. Fu Jian named them one by one. At Manu’s name, Fu Rong slowly shut his eyes, recalling the year when men mocked the Qiang soldier’s accent and Wang Meng punished them by making them repair the ditch together. The old soldier had now saved his commander, his accent scattered in the wind.
“If Helai Yan were still alive,” Fu Rong said slowly, “he’d say the four of us make more noise arguing than fighting.”

Fu Jian held his hand without taking up the joke. That name had entered the list of fallen men years before. He remembered how often people had warned, when they first created the mixed battalions, that soldiers of different peoples would never trust one another in battle. If Liang Hu, Manu, Zhai Hei, and Zhao An had each stayed with his own men looking for help, Fu Rong might already have been buried on the riverbank.
“Brother,” Fu Rong said softly, “don’t cross the river in pursuit tonight.”
“The order has already gone out.”
Fu Rong looked at the roof of the tent. After a long silence he said, “Then this leg of mine has ached for something worthwhile.”

At roll call that night some Qin soldiers were missing, and wounded Beifu men had been rescued. Both armies retrieved their dead. Fu Jian instructed the Qin force upstream to hold the ferry it had seized, not to cut off Liu Yu’s returning boats along the river. On the following day, if the Jin agreed, the two sides would exchange the dead whose identities could be established. Some soldiers were dissatisfied: letting Liu Yu escape, they said, might mean disaster later. Fu Jian sat outside the wounded men’s camp and finished an order for replenishing grain before he looked up. “There will be battles enough in days to come. If we lower the red flag because we’ve won one today, these twenty years must be lived all over again.”

The wind passed through the arrow holes in the torn banner. Its guard straightened the pole and the next watch took over. Fu Rong’s dead horse lay on the shoals until dawn, when it would be dragged away and buried. A wounded soldier stared at it a long time. “To think the general came out from under that horse,” he said. Another answered that the standard-bearer had held firm, and that several others had been there too. The wounded man wanted to know their names, but his stretcher was carried away before he could hear them all.

Darkness returned to both banks of the Fei. The mud where the horse had fallen was still warm; the holes torn through the banner had dried. Along the bank, sentries relieved one another, passing the flagstaff from hand to hand, and waited for the wind of another night.
